Situation: I was delivering a GKE platform for a fictional logistics firm, Harborline, with colleagues five and a half hours ahead of me, and work kept stalling waiting for answers. Task: keep progress continuous. Action: we agreed an end-of-day handoff note in a shared channel covering what was done, what was blocked, and the question needing an answer. We kept a thirty-minute daily overlap for decisions only. I moved design discussions into short written proposals in pull request descriptions, so either side could review asynchronously. Result: work moved forward almost around the clock, waiting time for answers fell sharply, and we delivered a week early. Lesson: in distributed teams, clear written handoffs matter more than more meetings, and I now set up the handoff format on day one.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Teamwork and Mentoring
question: Behavioural: Describe a time you shared knowledge from a customer engagement with the rest of your team.
answer: I turned lessons from a difficult RAG deployment into a short internal guide and a session that other engineers used on their projects. Situation: at a fictional healthcare company, Fernvale Health, I learned several non-obvious lessons about document ingestion: scanned PDFs, tables, and version control of policies. Task: stop colleagues from repeating the same mistakes. Action: I wrote a two-page ingestion checklist with concrete checks, such as running OCR quality sampling with Document AI before indexing and storing effective dates as metadata, and added anonymised examples. I presented it in our team's weekly knowledge-share session and put it in our shared repository with a template evaluation set. Result: three colleagues used the checklist on their next engagements, and one reported catching a scanned-document problem in week one instead of week five. Lesson: writing down lessons while they are fresh multiplies their value, so I now schedule it in the final week of every engagement.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Teamwork and Mentoring
question: Behavioural: You are asked to lead a newly formed team of engineers you have never worked with on a high-stakes customer deployment. How do you get them working well quickly?
answer: I would establish clear goals, roles and working norms in the first week, learn each person's strengths, and create early wins together. Situation: I led four engineers from different teams to build an AI document-processing platform for a fictional bank, Quillstone Bank, over twelve weeks. Task: make them effective quickly under scrutiny. Action: in the first two days, I held one-to-ones to learn each person's experience and goals, then ran a kickoff where we agreed the customer outcome, workstream owners, a definition of done, and review norms. I chose a first milestone achievable in ten days, a working ingestion path in a development project, so the team succeeded together early. I held short daily stand-ups and a weekly retrospective. Result: the team hit the first milestone, delivered the platform on time, and two members asked to work together again. Lesson: an early shared win builds trust faster than any team-building exercise.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Teamwork and Mentoring
question: Behavioural: Tell me about a time you gave difficult feedback to a peer.
answer: I gave a respected peer direct feedback about how he treated customer engineers, focusing on specific behaviour and its impact. Situation: on a joint engagement at a fictional energy company, Corvana Energy, a senior colleague often dismissed customer engineers' questions in meetings, and two of them stopped speaking up. Task: address it without damaging our relationship. Action: I asked for a private conversation, described two specific moments, and explained the effect I had observed: the customer engineers had stopped raising issues, which put the handover at risk. I asked how he saw it. He had not realised and explained he was under deadline pressure. We agreed he would route detailed questions to a written thread where he could answer properly. Result: the customer engineers became more engaged, and he later thanked me. Lesson: describing specific behaviour and its impact, rather than character, makes difficult feedback hearable, and I should have raised it after the first instance.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Teamwork and Mentoring
question: Behavioural: You are the most senior engineer on site, and a customer executive asks you to assess whether their internal platform team is capable of running the AI platform. How do you handle it?
answer: I would give an honest, evidence-based assessment focused on capabilities and gaps rather than individuals, and share it in a way that helps the team rather than threatening it. Situation: the CTO of a fictional manufacturer, Ironbridge Components, asked me privately whether his platform team could take over our GKE and Vertex AI platform. Task: answer truthfully without becoming an informal performance reviewer. Action: I agreed to assess capabilities, not people, and told the platform lead openly what I had been asked. I assessed against concrete areas: Terraform and GitOps practice, Kubernetes operations, incident response, and AI-specific skills like evaluation and model updates, using evidence from our work together. The report showed strengths in infrastructure and gaps in evaluation and on-call. I recommended a training plan and a three-month shadowing period. Result: the CTO funded the plan, and the team took over successfully. Lesson: transparency with the assessed team turns an awkward request into a development plan.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Motivation and Role Fit
question: Behavioural: Why do you want to work as a Forward Deployed Engineer rather than in a traditional platform or product engineering team?
answer: I want the FDE role because I do my best work close to real users, where I can see a problem, build a solution, and watch it change how people work. Situation: in my platform engineering work, the projects I enjoyed most were the ones where I sat with users, such as building a RAG assistant with dispatchers at a fictional logistics firm, Harborline. Task: I wanted more of that direct impact. Action: I volunteered for customer-facing work, ran discovery sessions, and handled deployments end to end, from Terraform foundations to GKE workloads to evaluation of AI behaviour. Result: those projects had the clearest measurable outcomes in my career, such as halving lookup time for dispatchers, and customer feedback was the most rewarding part of my work. The FDE role combines the engineering depth I have with the customer contact I value. Lesson: I learned that I am motivated by visible outcomes, and I look for roles that keep me close to them.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Motivation and Role Fit
question: Behavioural: How do you feel about frequent travel and working on site with customers? Give an example of how you have managed it.
answer: I am comfortable with regular travel and see on-site time as valuable, as long as it is planned around clear goals. Situation: on an engagement with a fictional manufacturer, Ironbridge Components, I travelled to their site every other week for three months. Task: make the travel worthwhile and sustainable. Action: I used on-site days for work that benefits from being in the room, such as discovery workshops, shadowing operators, whiteboard design sessions, and building relationships with their platform team. Remote days were for focused engineering: Terraform modules, pipeline work, and code reviews. I planned trips with the customer in advance and kept a consistent routine so travel did not erode my sleep or exercise. Result: the on-site sessions resolved decisions much faster than calls had, and I stayed productive throughout. Lesson: travel is most valuable when on-site time is reserved for things that only work face to face.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Motivation and Role Fit
question: Behavioural: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new technology very quickly for a customer.
answer: I learned enough Document AI in about a week to deliver a working extraction pipeline for a customer pilot. Situation: a fictional insurer, Corvane Mutual, needed claim forms processed automatically, and I had never used Document AI. Task: be credible with the customer within days. Action: I worked through the official quickstarts, built a throwaway prototype on a sample of twenty anonymised forms, and wrote down what worked and what did not. I asked a colleague who had used it for a thirty-minute review of my approach, which saved me from a processor choice that would not have handled their handwritten fields. I was honest with the customer that I was new to the service but showed the prototype. Result: the pilot pipeline on Cloud Run extracted the key fields accurately on most forms, and the customer approved the next phase. Lesson: a quick prototype plus one expert review is the fastest way I know to learn safely.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Motivation and Role Fit
question: Behavioural: How do you manage constant context switching between customers, technologies and internal work? Give an example.
answer: I manage context switching by batching work by customer, keeping a written context log per engagement, and protecting focus blocks. Situation: at one point I supported three customers at once: a GKE migration, a RAG pilot, and a Terraform landing zone. Task: stay effective without dropping details. Action: I assigned customers to specific days or half days where possible, and kept a short running log per customer with open decisions, next actions, and recent changes, which I reviewed for two minutes before switching. I blocked two mornings a week for deep engineering work with notifications off, and used one shared task board so nothing lived only in my head. I told each customer my availability pattern so they knew when to expect responses. Result: I delivered all three on schedule, and customers said response times felt predictable. Lesson: writing context down is what makes switching cheap, and I should have set up the logs before taking on the third customer.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Motivation and Role Fit
question: Behavioural: You are placed with a customer whose technology stack you have never used, such as Azure instead of GCP. How do you become effective in the first two weeks?
answer: I would map the concepts I know to their stack, focus on the parts that matter for the deployment, and be honest about what I am learning while delivering early value. Situation: I was assigned to a fictional retailer, Ridgepoint Retail, running on Azure, while my experience was mainly GCP. Task: become credible quickly. Action: in the first days I mapped equivalents, GKE to AKS, Cloud Run to Azure Container Apps, IAM and Workload Identity to Entra ID and managed identities, and Terraform providers from google to azurerm. I asked their engineers to walk me through their existing setup and pair on the first changes. I took a task I could deliver well, containerising and deploying the RAG service through their pipeline, while learning the rest. Result: I shipped the first deployment in week two, and their team valued my Kubernetes and evaluation experience regardless of cloud. Lesson: fundamentals transfer across clouds, and asking to be shown their setup builds trust faster than pretending to know it.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Motivation and Role Fit
question: Behavioural: Tell me about a time you felt burned out or overloaded in a demanding role and what you did about it.
answer: I recognised early signs of overload, raised it with my manager with a concrete proposal, and changed how I worked. Situation: during a period with two concurrent customer launches and on-call duty, I was working late most nights, and my code review quality was slipping. Task: recover without letting customers down. Action: I listed my commitments with effort estimates and showed my manager that they exceeded my capacity by roughly a third. I proposed handing on-call for one customer to a colleague for a month and pushing a non-urgent internal project. I also set firmer boundaries: no work messages after a set time except pages, and a proper break each day. Result: both launches went well, my review quality recovered, and my manager adjusted how engagements were staffed for the team. Lesson: raising capacity problems with data and a proposal is professional rather than weak, and I now check my load every two weeks.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Motivation and Role Fit
question: Behavioural: Where do you see yourself growing as a Forward Deployed Engineer over the next few years, and what have you already done towards it?
answer: I want to grow into someone who leads complex, multi-team AI deployments and shapes the platform from field experience, and I have already started on both. Situation: in recent work I moved from delivering individual components to owning whole engagements, such as a RAG platform for a fictional bank, Quillstone Bank, covering discovery, Terraform foundations, GKE serving, and evaluation. Task: build the skills for broader leadership. Action: I have led small teams on two engagements, mentored junior engineers, contributed reusable modules to our platform, and written field reports that influenced product defaults. I am deepening multi-cloud skills, practising on AWS and Azure equivalents, and studying agent evaluation and safety. Result: I now lead discovery and executive conversations independently, and colleagues use my Terraform blueprint and ingestion checklist. Over the next few years I want to lead larger programmes and mentor other FDEs. Lesson: growth came fastest when I volunteered for the uncomfortable parts, so I deliberately keep doing that.

category: Customer-Facing and Behavioural (FDE) - Motivation and Role Fit
question: Behavioural: Midway through a long engagement, the customer asks you to join them full time. How do you handle the offer professionally?
answer: I would thank them, avoid any commitment on the spot, tell my manager promptly, and make sure the engagement is not affected whatever I decide. Situation: the head of engineering at a fictional logistics firm, Harborline, offered me a role during a six-month platform engagement. Task: handle it with integrity towards both organisations. Action: I said I appreciated it and would need to think and follow my employer's policies. That week I told my manager openly and checked the non-solicitation terms in our contract, which restricted hiring for a period. I considered my goals honestly: I valued the variety of the FDE role more than depth at one company. I declined politely, explained why, and suggested how they could hire for the role, including the skills to look for. Result: the relationship stayed strong, they hired a strong internal candidate whom I helped onboard, and they renewed our engagement. Lesson: transparency with my own manager is what keeps an offer like this from becoming a conflict of interest.
